Simulate experience data from a mortality

Source: R/simulate.R
simulate.Rd

Draws a death time for every life in a population under a known mortality, and returns the result as an exp_data() with the same shape as real data: E2R_start, E2R_end and E2R_died, and every other column the population came with. A fit to the result can then be judged against the mortality that made it.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'mortality'
simulate(
  object,
  nsim = 1,
  seed = NULL,
  lives,
  exp_start,
  exp_end,
  time_scale = default_time_scale,
  ...
)

Arguments

object

The mortality to simulate from: any mortality, including a fitted model's $mortality and a mortality() expression switching on the population's columns.

nsim

How many datasets to draw. One returns an exp_data; more returns a list of them.

seed

Passed to set.seed() first when not NULL.

lives

The population. See The population.

exp_start, exp_end

The experience period, as dateys or years.

time_scale

The step of the hazard grid, as in settings().

...

Ignored.

Value

An exp_data(), or a list of nsim of them.

The population

lives is a data frame (or list of columns) with a birth column of dateys, whatever covariate columns the mortality and any later analysis need, and two optional datey columns:

  • E2R_start – when each life's exposure begins: retirement, joining, the first date the record is reliable. Absent, every life starts at exp_start. A life is alive at its start by construction, which is the left-truncation the E2R framework assumes.

  • E2R_cap – the date a life would leave observation for a reason other than death: withdrawal, transfer out, a record closed. NA means no such date. Absent, no life has one.

Each life is observed from max(E2R_start, exp_start) to the earliest of its death, its E2R_cap and exp_end. A death before the cap is a death and the cap plays no part; a life still alive at the cap is censored there. Lives with no observation at all are dropped, with a message saying how many. E2R_cap is dropped from the result, so that simulated data has exactly the columns real data has. Names beginning E2R_ are reserved and cannot be read by a pronoun expression, so it could not have leaked into a calculation either way.

How deaths are drawn

Each life gets a target \(-\log U\) for uniform \(U\), and dies where its cumulative hazard \(\int\mu\,dt\) from its start first reaches it. The hazard is accumulated on the same grid the engine integrates on: from the life's own start in steps of time_scale, \(\mu\) read at each step's midpoint, a shorter final step to the cap, and the death placed within the crossing step at the constant hazard of that step. So a fit to simulated data is unbiased against the mortality that made it, up to sampling noise.

A death is recorded to the day it fell on, at datey::mid_day(), exactly as a real death is. Deaths are independent across lives with no extra variation, so the data is Poisson-like: an overdispersion of 1 is the truth for it.

Reproducibility

The targets are drawn with R's own generator, so set.seed() before the call, or the seed argument, makes the result repeatable.

Examples

set.seed(1)
lives <- data.frame(
  birth   = datey::datey(2015 - sample(60:85, 500, replace = TRUE)),
  sex     = sample(c("male", "female"), 500, replace = TRUE),
  pension = round(rlnorm(500, log(12000), 0.7))
)

male <- gompertz_mortality(log_mu_0 = -3.6)
female <- gompertz_mortality(log_mu_0 = -4.0)
truth <- mortality(if (.i$sex == "male") male else female)

data <- simulate(truth, lives = lives,
                 exp_start = datey::datey(2015), exp_end = datey::datey(2020))
data
#> # Exp data: 500 × 6 (5 yr)
#> #   Start:  2015-01-01.0
#> #   End:    2020-01-01.0
#>           birth sex    pension    E2R_start      E2R_end E2R_died
#>         <datey> <chr>    <dbl>      <datey>      <datey> <lgl>   
#>  1 1931-01-01.0 female   15426 2015-01-01.0 2015-04-25.5 TRUE    
#>  2 1952-01-01.0 male     10470 2015-01-01.0 2015-11-28.5 TRUE    
#>  3 1949-01-01.0 female    9759 2015-01-01.0 2020-01-01.0 FALSE   
#>  4 1955-01-01.0 female   16989 2015-01-01.0 2020-01-01.0 FALSE   
#>  5 1954-01-01.0 female   16850 2015-01-01.0 2020-01-01.0 FALSE   
#>  6 1933-01-01.0 male     12159 2015-01-01.0 2020-01-01.0 FALSE   
#>  7 1945-01-01.0 male     18714 2015-01-01.0 2020-01-01.0 FALSE   
#>  8 1942-01-01.0 male     20349 2015-01-01.0 2019-03-08.5 TRUE    
#>  9 1938-01-01.0 male     21508 2015-01-01.0 2019-07-11.5 TRUE    
#> 10 1937-01-01.0 female   23593 2015-01-01.0 2020-01-01.0 FALSE   
#> # ℹ 490 more rows

# The data is neutral against the mortality that made it, within noise.
aev(data, mortality = truth, overdispersion = 1)
#> <aev[1]>
#>    A        E        V      A/E  95% conf dev resid
#> 1 73 66.88376 66.88376 1.091446 0.2396557 0.7368819
